items: "Why do I need to deliver my baby early?"

blocks.text: "Your blood pressure and the changes we are seeing indicate that the pregnancy is affecting your health. Severe pre-eclampsia can affect important organs such as the brain, kidneys, liver and lungs, and it can also affect the baby's blood and oxygen supply through the placenta. Our first priority is to stabilise you and monitor your baby closely. Depending on how you and your baby respond, we may need to deliver the baby earlier than planned because delivery is the definitive treatment for pre-eclampsia."

"At 28 weeks, if both mother and fetus are stable and there is no indication for immediate delivery, management may sometimes be expectant in a specialist centre with intensive maternal and fetal surveillance. However, maternal or fetal deterioration would necessitate delivery."

"This is severe pre-eclampsia and I would treat it as an obstetric emergency. I would call for senior obstetric and anaesthetic assistance and assess and stabilise the mother using an ABCDE approach. I would urgently treat severe hypertension with an appropriate antihypertensive agent, administer magnesium sulfate for seizure prophylaxis where indicated, and carefully monitor reflexes, respiratory rate and urine output. I would obtain urgent FBC, renal and liver function tests and coagulation studies where indicated, establish appropriate IV access and carefully manage fluids because of the risk of pulmonary oedema. I would assess fetal wellbeing with CTG and ultrasound with Doppler assessment where appropriate, administer antenatal corticosteroids if preterm delivery is anticipated, and then determine the timing and mode of delivery based on maternal and fetal condition.
